endorsements.title: Development and preliminary testing of Health Equity Across the AI Lifecycle (HEAAL): A framework for healthcare delivery organizations to mitigate the risk of AI solutions worsening health inequities

endorsements.title: Proceedings of the second Artificial Intelligence in Primary Immunodeficiency (AIPI) meeting
endorsements.issuer: The Journal of allergy and clinical immunology
endorsements.quote: The latter involves proactive patient outreach to confirm diagnoses.

commentary.bottom_line: Two sources, the HEAAL framework and the AIPI meeting proceedings, endorse prospective equity assessment with diagnostic outreach to all high-risk patients, but no supplied study tests this practice or documents the hazard it targets. The recommendation currently rests on expert reasoning alone.

perspectives.view: No study in the supplied set tests prospective outreach-based equity assessment, and no study documents how often biased historical labels hide underperformance. Both endorsements are a framework and a meeting commentary. Under GRADE conventions, expert statements without supporting data cannot establish certainty, so the effect of the practice on detecting missed underperformance remains unknown.

The practice aims to correct underdiagnosis in disadvantaged groups. No supplied study measures whether outreach to all high-risk patients reveals performance gaps in Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The groups the recommendation intends to protect therefore have no direct evidence showing that the approach works for them.

commentary.research_gap: Prospective studies are needed that deploy a model, conduct diagnostic workup on all high-risk patients regardless of prior diagnosis, and compare subgroup performance estimates from that confirmed-diagnosis cohort against estimates from historical labels. Such studies should also report outreach completion rates, workup costs, and staffing requirements by patient group.
commentary.underserved_note: No supplied study tested the practice in any population, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. Health systems adopting the practice for these groups would be acting on expert judgment and should plan to collect subgroup outcome data from the start.
